region.name: Southwestern Amazon (Rondônia)
region.setting: Tropical rainforest with extensive land clearing since the 1980s. The box covers the Brazilian state of Rondônia and neighbouring parts of Bolivia and of other Brazilian states.

variable.name: Precipitation
variable.definition: Average rain and melted snow reaching the surface each day. MERRA-2 adjusts its modelled precipitation toward gauge and satellite observations.

verdict.title: Significant falling trend that holds across date ranges
verdict.text: Over 1981-2025 the series changed by -0.541 mm/day per decade. Both significance tests agree after allowing for month-to-month persistence, and 100% of all date windows of 15+ years point the same way.

crosscheck.label: Second dataset agrees on direction, not size
crosscheck.text: GPCP v2.3, an independent record, shows −0.282 mm/day per decade (95% range −0.372 to −0.192): the same direction, but the two ranges do not overlap. The rate here is about 1.9 times as large. Treat the direction as supported and the size as uncertain.

dataset.name: GPCP v2.3
dataset.long_name: Global Precipitation Climatology Project (GPCP) Monthly Analysis, Version 2.3
dataset.kind: A merged analysis of satellite estimates and rain-gauge measurements, on a 2.5° grid.
dataset.citation: Adler, R. F., et al. (2018). The Global Precipitation Climatology Project (GPCP) Monthly Analysis (New Version 2.3) and a Review of 2017 Global Precipitation. Atmosphere, 9(4), 138. GPCP data provided by the NOAA PSL, Boulder, Colorado, USA, from https://psl.noaa.gov
dataset.caveat: GPCP cells are 2.5° wide, much coarser than the region boxes, and its rain-gauge input also changes over time. Agreement is support, not proof.

known_issue.title: Known data issue: MERRA-2 rainfall shifts in 2005

sources.label: Reichle et al. (2017), Land Surface Precipitation in MERRA-2, J. Climate 30(5), 1643–1664
Reichle (2023), The Land Surface in Earth System Reanalysis, slide 12 (NASA NTRS 20230012995)
Moreira et al. (2023), Climate 11(2), 27: rainfall trends in Rondônia from CHIRPS, 1981–2020

known_issue.credit: Found by the team's scientific validation review (SCIENTIFIC_VALIDATION.md).
known_issue.text: NASA's own evaluation of MERRA-2 rainfall (Reichle et al. 2017) shows its gauge-corrected rainfall dropping against GPCP across the Amazon (72.5°W–50°W, 12.5°S–2.5°N) from 2005, the year the number of rain gauges behind the correction falls sharply. NASA attributes such jumps to changes in the gauge product and the observing system, not to the weather. This region box shows the same shift: MERRA-2 ran 0.13 mm/day below GPCP v2.3 in 1981–2004 and 0.99 mm/day below GPCP v2.3 from 2005. Fitted as a jump in 2005 with a steady drift allowed, the jump is −1.07 mm/day (95% range −1.51 to −0.63), with no significant drift left between the two records. Taken separately, the two periods give −0.14 against −0.14 mm/day per decade before 2005 and −0.59 against −0.83 from 2005; in both periods the two records' 95% ranges overlap. So much of MERRA-2's faster full-record decline probably comes from how the dataset was built, not from rainfall. A detected trend is not a validated change: the direction is supported by both records, the size is not confirmed.

source.dataset: MERRA-2 (Modern-Era Retrospective analysis for Research and Applications, Version 2)
source.producer: NASA Global Modeling and Assimilation Office (GMAO)
source.access: NASA POWER Monthly and Annual API (NASA Langley Research Center)
source.kind: Reanalysis: a global model constrained by satellite and ground observations. Values are model-based estimates, not direct instrument readings.
source.caveat: MERRA-2 is a reanalysis: a model constrained by satellite and ground observations, not a direct measurement. Changes in the observing system over time (new satellites, fewer rain gauges) can create or hide trends, especially for precipitation and soil wetness. Check important results against an independent dataset.
